title: Why AI Coding Agents Lose Context After the PR, and How to Keep It
story_key: story|title:why ai coding agents lose context after the pr and how to keep it
content_excerpt: AI coding agents lose context once a PR enters the pipeline. See how code context and delivery context work An AI coding agent can read a repository, trace its dependencies, edit a dozen files, and open a pull request that passes its own tests. Then the PR enters the delivery pipeline, and much of what the agent learned stays behind. The pipeline produces evidence the agent never sees: a failed build, a vulnerable dependency flagged by a scan, a latency regression after deployment, an incident traced to a change that looked safe. That evidence could improve the original change and prevent the next failure, but only if something carries it back into the engineering workflow. Writing code is often no longer the slow part. Moving a change through build, test, security, deployment, and runtime is, and each of those stages is a question of risk. Context engineering across the SDLC is the work of connecting them. This post covers what context an agent needs, how the Code Context Engine and the Software Delivery Knowledge Graph supply two halves of it, and what works today and what Harness has said is planned. Context engineering is the work of selecting, organizing, retrieving, and maintaining what an AI agent knows while it works on a task. It covers more than prompt wording. An agent may need architectural decisions, dependency relationships, repository conventions, test results, security findings, deployment history, and operating constraints. Agent memory and context engineering do different jobs. Memory stores what might be useful across sessions. Context engineering decides what goes in front of the agent for the current task. A large memory store does not help when the retrieved material is outdated, contradictory, or irrelevant. Augment Code measured the effect of retrieval quality in its February 2026 Context Engine MCP benchmark . Its most useful finding concerns model choice: a weaker model with great context (Sonnet with the MCP) can outperform a stronger model with poor context (Opus without it). MCP-enabled runs also needed fewer tool calls and conversation turns. The test ran 300 Elasticsearch pull requests with three prompts each, 900 attempts in total, scored on correctness, completeness, best practices, code reuse, and unsolicited documentation. Adding the Code Context Engine improved results by 80% for Claude Code, 71% for Cursor, and 30% for Cursor with Composer-1 . title: Towards Verifiable LLM Infra
content_excerpt: Coding agents are getting remarkably good at writing LLM infrastructure, from GPU kernels and schedulers to custom serving engines. Suppose an AI agent is strong enough to build a fast inference engine from scratch; in this second half of the problem, the bottleneck shifts from capability to verification : how do we know the engine it wrote is actually correct? Passing latency and throughput benchmarks still leaves rare concurrency bugs hidden. As a single engineer begins orchestrating 100, 1,000, or even 10,000 coding agents in parallel, human code review hits a hard cognitive wall. Having agents review other agents does not solve this either; as pstack author Lauren Tan noted , adversarial reviews are mostly a waste of tokens, and it is far better to spend those tokens on empirical and formal verification. In this post, we introduce vstack , a 5-stage formal verification workflow for coding agents, and veriserve , a prototype verifiable LLM serving engine with PD disaggregation built around a formally verified KV-page lifecycle design model. Applying vstack to production Prefill-Decode serving uncovered three classes of real RDMA and cache concurrency bugs across SGLang and vLLM, resulting in 6 proposed upstream pull requests . Meanwhile, veriserve backs its PdLedger design model with a 226-module, 516,973-obligation TLAPS safety proof while adding only 0.18% mean p50 TPOT overhead on NVIDIA GB200. We believe verifiable serving defines the second half of LLM infra as autonomous coding agents write the deepest layers of production systems. Why is verifying an LLM serving engine so hard in the first place? Over the past three years, inference engines like vLLM and SGLang have evolved from single-node executors into asynchronous distributed systems, layering paged KV memory , shared prefix caching , and disaggregated prefill-decode RDMA transfers over the same pool of physical GPU KV pages. When a request times out or aborts, its cleanup now races across RDMA network cards, CPU cache trees, and GPU attention kernels simultaneously. Because GPUDirect RDMA writes directly into GPU memory without involving the target CPU, a lifecycle mismatch often does not crash the server, but returns HTTP 200 OK while silently mixing one user’s KV cache into another user’s response. title: Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams
story_key: story|title:worse together how performance breaks down in multi user multi agent teams
content_excerpt: As AI agents become more capable and widely used, they are increasingly required to interact with each other. Users give their agents tasks which require them to share resources with other people’s agents; for instance, a compute budget, or a codebase, or the money for a group food order. These settings are understudied, so we built four environments with simulated users and everyday tasks and tested frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Alibaba in them. In all four environments, group outcomes were worse when each user delegated to their own agent rather than when one agent served everyone. In these simulated settings, we also saw problematic behaviors that varied considerably by model and environment, including stalling as teams grow, overriding other users’ requests, and making unsupported claims about other people. Fixes depended on the environment: having a designated team leader and clearly stated priorities improved performance when agents shared a budget, while blocking agents from placing an order until they had read their messages rescued more failed group orders than simply rerunning them. We are releasing three of the environments as a benchmark, MAMUBench, so that others can use them to test how well agents coordinate, and how they behave, in multi-user, multi-agent systems. As AI agents become more common, users increasingly deploy them to pursue goals that require interacting with other agents. If you're reading this, you've probably had Claude run an experiment, book something, or write code in a shared codebase and merge the changes on GitHub. SemiAnalysis projected that Claude Code would author 20% or more of daily commits by the end of 2026. Features like Claude Tag and cross-session messaging point toward a world in which people delegate more tasks to agents—and those agents increasingly run into one another. Recent releases also let several users share resources through their agents: with the DoorDash CLI , several people's agents can add to one group cart; Slack Code brings agents such as Claude, Devin and GitHub Copilot into channels the whole team works in; and OpenAI's dots give each person an agent that works on their behalf, in a space shared with teammates ( DevDay 2026 recap ). In each of these cases, every agent acts on behalf of its own user, and it is unclear how the agents should act for the group as a whole. title: From Process Models to Composable Agentic Workflows: Combining BPMN, Agents and Enterprise Knowledge
summary:
LLM-based agents can reason, use tools and collaborate. However, coordinating increasingly complex agentic applications becomes difficult to understand, monitor and improve. Decisions distributed across prompts, tool calls and application logic make workflows implicit. We introduce **Recursive Capability Composition**, enabling agents to execute business processes and expose them as reusable Agentic Tools.
  This paper presents a BPMN-based approach to Agentic Workflows, combining explicit orchestration with autonomous reasoning. SemTalk BPMN models are transformed into executable workflows using a LangGraph/Pregel runtime. Agentic Tasks introduce LLM reasoning at selected activities, while conventional BPMN controls process flows, deterministic decisions, system interactions and human approvals. Agentic Participants provide reusable interfaces for agent behavior or other executable processes.
  BPMN orchestration makes multi-agent systems more understandable and manageable. Explicit process models provide developers and operators with a shared view of workflow structures and execution progress, facilitating debugging, monitoring and optimization.
  Enterprise agents also need organization-specific context. Process Models and Knowledge Graphs describe activities, participants, information objects, decisions and relationships between processes. They provide structured knowledge of how an organization operates, supporting informed agent decisions and actions.
  Our contributions are threefold: 1. **Model-Driven Execution:** Transforming BPMN models into executable Agentic Workflows. 2. **Recursive Capability Composition:** Exposing agents and executable business processes as reusable tools for other agents. 3. **Enterprise Context:** Using Process Models and Ontologies to provide organization-specific knowledge for agent reasoning.

title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available

also_covered.title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics Control, Simulation, and Policy Improvement

content_excerpt: Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. title: Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study of Where Errors Enter and Which Controls Reach Them
summary: When an LLM agent fails part-way through a long task, the usual analysis records a symptom: a failure-mode label, or the agent and step judged responsible. It does not say where the error entered, which state carried it to the symptom, whether anything in the trajectory contradicted it, or which control could have caught it. We define an episode record that ties a candidate fault to its origin, propagation, detection, response and consequence, located by operational phase and state domain, and that names the control families whose observation and reach cover it. We turned the record into a written annotation protocol and applied it to 95 failed runs of six multi-agent systems from the public Who&When and MAD corpora, reading each trajectory in full. Faults enter early (median at 0.18 of the run), mostly as wrong decisions or fabrications over task state, and in 37 of 88 Who&When runs before the step the corpus' human labels mark as decisive. In 72% of failed runs the trajectory already contained evidence against the error before the failure; in 88% of those no agent acted on it. Something flagged a deviation in 31% of runs, but no response removed the deviated state. Independent judges reading the unused evidence, task contracts fixed at admission, and re-checking beliefs against the environment reach most episodes; restoring the agent's own state would have sufficed in 35 of 95 runs. A text scan of the raw corpus also shows that 45% of the hand-crafted Who&When failures ended with a provider content-filter crash after which the harness emitted a final answer no agent produced, a failure class that neither symptom taxonomies nor responsible-agent labels represent. Protocol, records and scripts are included.

title: Forward-Value Discretization: Faster Stochastic Diffusion Sampling Without High-Order Approximation
summary: Stochastic diffusion samplers often require substantially more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic samplers to achieve comparable sample quality. Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DDPM.

title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
summary: Eval-driven development helps you build AI agents against a consistent set of metrics. Define good behavior, write the eval first, then compare experiments.
story_key: story|title:what is eval driven development how to improve ai agents
content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
summary: Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send.
story_key: story|title:designing for agents zeno rocha resend
content_excerpt: Keyword matches words; semantic matches meaning and exact titles or names; hybrid combines both. In keyword mode, use quotation marks for exact phrases. Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send. Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request

title: Causal Concept Explanations for Deep Neural Models
summary: Concept-based explanations in neural models are important for the development, certification, and adoption of autonomous systems. Yet, interpretability remains correlational. Without methods to guide and quantify causal relationships between explanations, a concept explanation can be provided without being necessary or sufficient for the observed output thereby appearing correct while misleading. We introduce Causal Concept Wrapper Network (CCW-Net), the first use of interventional mediation analysis from fields such as economics, medicine, and epidemiology as a training objective to align causal effects of concept-based explanations with a model's output. We further apply mediation analysis as an evaluation tool to quantify, per concept label combination, how much of any model's output is causally attributable to each concept explanation. As a training objective, CCW-Net shapes a model's concept representations such that they are both necessary and sufficient for the outputs they are credited with and independent of other concepts' contributions. Counterfactual concept representations anchor a set of causal alignment criteria: necessity, sufficiency, and independence. Necessity drives irrelevant concept effects toward zero, sufficiency ensures relevant concept representations fully reconstruct a model's output, and independence enforces the total effect decomposes linearly across concepts. We evaluate CCW-Net across aircraft control, driving, and image classification. CCW-Net provides a step toward concept-based explanations that are not merely interpretable, but quantifiably causal, supporting safer evaluation, certification, and deployment of transparent and trustworthy neural models.
